clue.text: Young offender pinned down by Behan

definitions.meaning: an inmate of a British reform institution for young criminals
the title of Brendan Behan's autobiographical book, whose story he set down in writing

explanation.surface: A juvenile delinquent is held down by someone called Behan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinned down' suggests a physical struggle, but it means written down: Brendan Behan's memoir of his time in a British reform school carries this title. A borstal was a British detention centre for young offenders.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses name the same thing: a lad held in a British youth detention centre, and Behan's memoir about being one.

clue.text: Explosive subject treated by "Frank" Harris

definitions.meaning: a device that blows up, used here as a noun
Frank Harris wrote a 1908 novel about the Haymarket anarchists with this title

explanation.surface: A touchy topic is handled with candour by someone named Harris.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks round 'Frank' make it look like an adjective for candour, but it is Harris's first name; his novel on the Chicago Haymarket affair has this title.
explanation.definitionFit: A device that detonates, and the title of Frank Harris's novel about anarchist violence.

clue.text: US poet meets Eastern children's writer

parts.note: John Crowe Ransom was an American poet and critic
E is the standard abbreviation for East or Eastern

explanation.surface: An American poet encounters an author of books for young readers.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Ransome wrote Swallows and Amazons and other books for young readers.

clue.text: 8's play exists in foreign language versions

definitions.meaning: Brian Friel, the answer to 8-down, wrote a 1980 play with this title about the mapping of Ireland
renderings of a text into other tongues

explanation.surface: A dramatist's work is available in editions in other tongues.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the play has been translated; in fact the play's title is that very word, and the clue's second half defines it in its ordinary sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Friel's play about Irish place-names carries this title, and versions of a text in other tongues are what the word ordinarily means.

clue.text: It accompanied present from Coward

parts.note: Noël Coward's comedy title pairs the word 'Present' with the word wanted here, so it comes along with 'present' in his title

explanation.surface: Something came along with a gift sent by a timid person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' reads as a gift and 'Coward' as a timid giver, but Coward is Noël Coward and 'Present' is the first word of his comedy title.
explanation.definitionFit: Coward's play title couples 'Present' with this word for amusement and mirth.

clue.text: Dramatist is enough to make a person unwell

parts.note: one can stand for a person, as in 'one does one's best'
unwell means ill

explanation.surface: A playwright is all it takes to make somebody feel sick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is enough to make' only links the two halves. The dramatist is Eugene O'Neill; the apostrophe is dropped in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugene O'Neill was an American playwright, author of Long Day's Journey into Night.

clue.text: Macbeth made one in the dark

definitions.text: Macbeth made one in the dark

parts.words: Macbeth made one in the dark
parts.note: Macbeth knifed Duncan at night, and a guess is proverbially made this way 'in the dark'

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's Macbeth commits his deed under cover of night.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'a ... in the dark' means a wild guess; Macbeth literally made such a knife thrust when he murdered Duncan at night.
explanation.definitionFit: A knife thrust, which Macbeth delivered to Duncan by night, and the idiom for a blind guess.

clue.text: God, supported only by water somewhere in France, like early ecologist

indicators.note: in a down answer the god sits on top and is held up from below by the next piece

parts.note: Thor is the Norse god of thunder
eau is the French word for water

explanation.surface: A deity resting on nothing but French water resembles an early environmentalist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supported only by' places THOR above EAU in the down light. Henry David Thoreau wrote Walden, about living close to nature.
explanation.definitionFit: Thoreau's Walden is often counted among the founding texts of environmental thought.

clue.text: Deviously infer Blair is Irish playwright

indicators.note: acting deviously means taking a crooked route, so the letters of the following words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Slyly conclude that a former prime minister is an Irish dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deviously' rearranges the letters of INFER and BLAIR; 'is' is a link. Blair the politician is a distraction.
explanation.definitionFit: Brian Friel, from Northern Ireland, wrote Translations and Dancing at Lughnasa.

clue.text: May they cause enthusiasts to lose sight of the bigger picture?

definitions.text: May they cause enthusiasts to lose sight of the bigger picture?

parts.words: May they cause enthusiasts to lose sight of the bigger picture?
parts.note: small paintings could lead collectors to ignore large canvases, punning on the idiom for missing the overall view

explanation.surface: A question whether fans of something become too narrow in their view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The bigger picture' is an idiom for the overall view, but here it is literal: collectors of tiny paintings might neglect large ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiny painted portraits, the opposite of a large canvas or 'bigger picture'.

clue.text: A great deal I got from creative French naval officer

parts.note: a lot means a great deal

explanation.surface: Someone gained plenty from an imaginative officer of the French navy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got from' links the wordplay to the definition. Pierre Loti was the pen name of Julien Viaud, a French naval officer who wrote novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierre Loti, author of Pêcheur d'Islande, was both a naval officer and a novelist, hence 'creative'.

clue.text: This is the way all the girls carry on in Jonathan Miller hit

definitions.text: This is the way all the girls carry on
definitions.meaning: the Italian title of Mozart's opera means roughly 'all women behave like this'
Jonathan Miller directed a much-admired production of this Mozart opera

explanation.surface: A remark on how young women behave, found in a successful show by a British director.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is an English rendering of the opera's Italian title; Jonathan Miller was a British director famed for his opera productions.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mozart opera's title translates as a claim that every woman acts this way, and Miller staged a celebrated version.

clue.text: She took a realistic view of a girl's attachment

definitions.text: She took a realistic view of a girl's attachment

parts.words: She took a realistic view of a girl's attachment
parts.note: Anita ... Gentlemen Prefer Blondes has its heroine Lorelei value diamonds over romance, a hard-headed view of what a girl holds dear

explanation.surface: A woman was pragmatic about a young woman's fondness for someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attachment' suggests a romance; in Anita Loos's novel the heroine's attachment is to diamonds and money, which the author treats with clear-eyed humour.
explanation.definitionFit: Anita Loos wrote Gentlemen Prefer Blondes, a comic novel about a gold-digging heroine.

clue.text: Burns Night in verse

parts.note: Robert Burns wrote a poem about the festivities of 31 October, a night he described in verse

explanation.surface: The Scottish celebration of Robert Burns, done in poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: Burns Night is the 25 January supper for Robert Burns, but here it means a night of Burns's: his poem about the eve of All Saints.
explanation.definitionFit: Burns's poem of that title describes the customs of the night before All Saints' Day.

clue.text: Seriously undernourished Shakespearean actor

definitions.meaning: Robin, the tailor in A Midsummer Night's Dream, acts Moonshine in the mechanicals' play

explanation.surface: A severely underfed player of the Bard's roles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shakespearean actor' is not a real performer but a character who acts: Robin the tailor plays Moonshine in the mechanicals' play in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
explanation.definitionFit: A starving wretch, and the name of the tailor who acts in Shakespeare's play-within-a-play.

clue.text: Novel phenomena en route To the Lighthouse

definitions.meaning: Virginia Woolf's 1931 novel of six voices

definitions.text: phenomena en route To the Lighthouse
definitions.meaning: the swells of the sea crossed on a boat trip to a lighthouse, and To the Lighthouse is another Woolf novel

explanation.surface: Something new is seen on the voyage in Virginia Woolf's book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like an adjective meaning new, but it is a noun: Woolf's novel of this name; the second half pictures the sea crossing in her earlier book.
explanation.definitionFit: Woolf wrote a novel with this title, and swells of the sea are met on any trip by boat to a lighthouse.

clue.text: It's quicker, said Nash

parts.note: Ogden Nash's couplet 'Candy is dandy, but ... is quicker' compares sweets with strong drink as aids to seduction

explanation.surface: A poet remarks that something gets results faster.
explanation.walkthrough: Ogden Nash was an American writer of comic verse; his two-line 'Reflections on Ice-Breaking' says sweets work, but alcohol works faster.
explanation.definitionFit: Strong alcoholic drink, which Nash's comic couplet rates faster than sweets at breaking the ice.

clue.text: Extreme wing that helps make the Church cross

definitions.text: Extreme wing that helps make the Church cross

parts.words: Extreme wing that helps make the Church cross
parts.note: the arms of a cruciform church stick out sideways, turning its plan into a cross

explanation.surface: A radical faction that angers the Church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extreme wing' suggests a radical faction and 'cross' suggests angry, but the wing is a transverse arm of a church building that gives its floor plan a cross shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Either arm crossing the nave of a cruciform church, forming the cross shape.

clue.text: Le Carré' house

parts.note: John le Carré's 1989 spy novel is titled with the name of a country followed by the word House

explanation.surface: The home of the spy novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House' reads as le Carré's home, but it is the last word of his novel The ... House, so the answer is the first word of that title.
explanation.definitionFit: Le Carré's Cold War novel is named after this country and a house.

clue.text: Eponymous Fay Weldon heroine hides identity in powerful Disraeli character

indicators.note: the heroine's name hides the next piece inside itself, wrapping round it

parts.note: Sonia is the name of a heroine in Fay Weldon's fiction, as in The Heart of the Country
ID is the usual short form of identity, as on an ID card

explanation.surface: A novelist's title character conceals who she is within a commanding figure from Disraeli.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hides' makes the heroine's name a container. Sidonia is the wealthy, influential Jewish financier of Disraeli's Coningsby, hence 'powerful'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sidonia is the immensely rich, influential financier of Disraeli's novel Coningsby.

clue.text: Altering integral shape of instrument

indicators.note: altering something changes its form, so the next word's letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Changing the essential form of a musical instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Altering' rearranges INTEGRAL; 'shape of' is a link, and fits because the instrument is named for its three-sided shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A percussion instrument made from a steel rod bent into three sides and struck with a beater.

clue.text: British cardinal's basis of belief

annotationWithheld.why: 'British cardinal's basis of belief': 'basis of belief' defines GROUNDS but no reading of 'British cardinal's' gives those letters or a cryptic sense that could be confirmed

clue.text: "Her knowledge … as valueless as old-fashioned — ornaments" (Felix Holt)

definitions.text: "Her knowledge … as valueless as old-fashioned — ornaments" (Felix Holt)

parts.words: "Her knowledge … as valueless as old-fashioned — ornaments" (Felix Holt)
parts.note: the dash in George Eliot's quotation from Felix Holt is filled by a kind of plaster once used for moulded decoration

explanation.surface: A quotation from George Eliot's Felix Holt with a word blanked out.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank: the missing word in George Eliot's sentence is a plaster used for decorative mouldings, out of fashion by her time.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine plaster for ceilings and walls, often moulded into decorative ornaments.

clue.text: Star-gazer featured in wedding tonight

indicators.note: the answer appears as a run of letters within the next words of the clue

explanation.surface: An astronomer is in the news for a marriage this evening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'featured in' shows the answer sitting inside 'wedding tonight'. Sir Arthur Eddington was a British astronomer.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Eddington was an astrophysicist who confirmed Einstein's prediction of starlight bending.

clue.text: NCO at scene of siege

definitions.meaning: Sergeant Frank ... is the dashing soldier in Hardy's Far from the Madding Crowd
the city besieged by the Greeks for ten years in Homer's Iliad

explanation.surface: A sergeant present where a city was blockaded.
explanation.walkthrough: An NCO is a non-commissioned officer; Hardy's Sergeant Troy is one, and the ancient city of the Trojan War has the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy's Sergeant shares his surname with the ancient city the Greeks besieged in the Iliad.

clue.text: Conscription of Italian novelist reported

indicators.note: a word that is reported is passed on by voice, so the name is replaced by one that sounds the same

parts.note: Primo Levi was an Italian writer, author of If This Is a Man

explanation.surface: The call-up of an author from Italy is in the news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reported' signals a soundalike: Primo LEVI is said like the word for raising troops; 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A levy is the compulsory enlisting of troops, as in raising a levy of soldiers.

clue.text: Maiden loved by Zeus not applicable in Christian site

parts.note: Io was a priestess loved by Zeus and turned into a heifer
N/A is the abbreviation for not applicable on forms

explanation.surface: A young woman Zeus adored is out of place at a holy spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link between wordplay and definition. Iona is the Hebridean island where St Columba founded his monastery.
explanation.definitionFit: Iona, off western Scotland, is where St Columba founded a monastery that spread the faith.

clue.text: Favourable reception in roman-fleuve writer's world

definitions.meaning: The ... World is a volume of Anthony Powell's novel sequence A Dance to the Music of Time

explanation.surface: A warm welcome in the world of an author of a long novel sequence.
explanation.walkthrough: A roman-fleuve is a sequence of linked novels; Anthony Powell's has a volume called The ... World, so the word goes in front of 'World'.
explanation.definitionFit: Approval or welcome, and the first word of a Powell title, The Acceptance World.

clue.text: Name of fellow in deteriorated portrait is Greek, yes?

definitions.text: Name of fellow in deteriorated portrait

parts.note: ay or aye is an old word for yes, as in voting

explanation.surface: A question whether a man in a decaying painting is from Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' links the definition to the wordplay. Oscar Wilde's Dorian Gray stays young while his painted portrait decays.
explanation.definitionFit: Dorian Gray, Wilde's hero, has a portrait that ages and decays in his place.

clue.text: "They are great parables — but false art ", said D. H. Lawrence of this man's works

definitions.text: "They are great parables — but false art ", said D. H. Lawrence of this man's works

parts.words: "They are great parables — but false art ", said D. H. Lawrence of this man's works
parts.note: D. H. Lawrence passed this judgement on the novels of the author of Crime and Punishment

explanation.surface: A critical verdict by D. H. Lawrence on another writer's books.
explanation.walkthrough: A literary-knowledge clue: Lawrence admired the Russian novelist's moral force but disliked his art.
explanation.definitionFit: Fyodor Dostoevsky, author of The Brothers Karamazov, whose novels Lawrence judged great parables.
